nodes.name: {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring}
nodes.statement: The {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring} problem is to test if a given graph allows a vertex-surjective homomorphism to a fixed graph~$\H$.
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether an input graph admits a vertex-surjective homomorphism to a fixed graph $\H$.

nodes.name: {\sc $\H$-Colouring} (homomorphism problem)
nodes.statement: The classical \emph{homomorphism problem}, also known as {\sc $\H$-Colouring}, involves a fixed structure~$\H$, with input another structure~$\G$, of the same signature, invoking the question as to whether there is a function from the domain of~$\G$ to the domain of $\H$ that is a homomorphism from $\G$ to $\H$.
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether an input structure $\G$ admits any homomorphism to a fixed structure $\H$.

nodes.name: Feder-Vardi dichotomy conjecture (proved by Bulatov and Zhuk)
nodes.statement: Their well-known conjecture, recently proved by Bulatov~\cite{FVproofBulatov} and Zhuk~\cite{FVproofZhuk}, stated that every CSP$(\H)$ has complexity either in P or \NP-complete, omitting any Ladner-like complexities in between.
nodes.statement_short: Every CSP$(\H)$ is either in P or \NP-complete, with no intermediate Ladner degrees.
nodes.origin_citation: Feder & Vardi; proved by Bulatov and Zhuk
assumptions: every CSP$(\H)$
conclusions: has complexity either in P or \NP-complete, omitting any Ladner-like complexities in between

nodes.name: {\sc $\H$-Compaction}
nodes.statement: Indeed, the {\sc $\H$-Compaction} problem, hitherto defined only for graphs~$\H$, takes as input a graph $\G$ and asks if there exists a function $f$ from $V(\G)$ to $V(\H)$ so that for each non-loop edge $(x,y) \in E(\H)$ (\mbox{i.e.} with $x\neq y$), there exists $u,v \in V(\G)$ so that $f(u)=x$ and $f(v)=y$.
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether an input graph maps onto $\H$ so that every non-loop edge of $\H$ is hit; the edge-surjective homomorphism problem.

nodes.name: {\sc $\H$-Retraction}
nodes.statement: The problem {\sc $\H$-Retraction} takes as input a superstructure~$\G$ of $\H$ and asks whether there is a homomorphism from $\G$ to $\H$ that is the identity on $\H$.
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a superstructure $\G$ of $\H$ admits a homomorphism to $\H$ fixing $\H$ pointwise.

nodes.name: {\sc List $\H$-colouring}
nodes.statement: The list homomorphism problem, {\sc List $\H$-colouring}, allows one to express restricted lists for each of the input structure's elements, that are the only domain elements permitted in a solution homomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: The homomorphism problem in which each input element carries a list restricting its permitted images.

nodes.name: Do Retraction, Compaction and Surjective Colouring always coincide in complexity?
nodes.statement: At present it is not known whether there is a graph $\H$ so that {\sc $\H$-Retraction}, {\sc $\H$-Compaction} and {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring} do not have the same complexity up to polynomial time reduction (see~\cite{CiE2017,VikasOther}).
nodes.statement_short: It is open whether some $\H$ separates {\sc $\H$-Retraction}, {\sc $\H$-Compaction} and {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring} up to polynomial-time reduction.

nodes.name: Bang-Jensen, Hell and MacGillivray dichotomy for irreflexive semicomplete digraphs
nodes.statement: In \cite{Semicomplete} Bang-Jensen, Hell, and MacGillivray proved that {\sc $\H$-Colouring} is always in \Ptime\ or is \NP-complete if $\H$ is irreflexive semicomplete.
nodes.statement_short: {\sc $\H$-Colouring} is in \Ptime\ or \NP-complete for irreflexive semicomplete $\H$.
assumptions: $\H$ is irreflexive semicomplete
conclusions: {\sc $\H$-Colouring} is always in \Ptime\ or is \NP-complete

nodes.name: Retraction classification for reflexive tournaments
nodes.statement: for a reflexive tournament~$\H$, the {\sc $\H$-Retraction} problem is in NL if $\H$ is transitive, and it is \NP-complete otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: {\sc $\H$-Retraction} is in NL for transitive reflexive tournaments and \NP-complete otherwise.
assumptions: for a reflexive tournament~$\H$
conclusions: the {\sc $\H$-Retraction} problem is in NL if $\H$ is transitive, and it is \NP-complete otherwise

nodes.name: forward-/backward-neighbour (adjacent)
nodes.statement: In a digraph $\G$, a forward- (resp., backward-) \emph{neighbour} (or \emph{adjacent}) to a vertex $u \in V(\G)$ is another vertex $v \in V(\G)$ so that $(u,v) \in E(\G)$ (resp., $(v,u) \in E(\G)$).
differentia: $(u,v) \in E(\G)$

nodes.name: out-degree and in-degree
nodes.statement: The \emph{out-degree} and \emph{in-degree} of a vertex are the number of its forward-neighbours and backward-neighbours, respectively.
nodes.genus: the number of its forward-neighbours and backward-neighbours

nodes.name: isolated vertex
nodes.statement: A vertex with out-degree and in-degree both 0 is said to be \emph{isolated}.
differentia: out-degree and in-degree both 0

nodes.name: reflexive / irreflexive vertex and digraph
nodes.statement: A vertex with a self-loop is \emph{reflexive} and otherwise it is \emph{irreflexive}. A digraph is \emph{(ir)reflexive} if all its vertices are (ir)reflexive.
differentia: all its vertices are (ir)reflexive

nodes.name: directed path on $k$ vertices
nodes.statement: The \emph{directed path} on $k$ vertices is the digraph with vertices $u_0,\ldots, u_{k-1}$ and edges $(u_i,u_{i+1})$ for $i=0,\ldots,k-2$.
differentia: vertices $u_0,\ldots, u_{k-1}$ and edges $(u_i,u_{i+1})$ for $i=0,\ldots,k-2$

nodes.name: directed cycle on $k$ vertices
nodes.statement: The \emph{directed cycle} on $k$ vertices is obtained from the directed path on $k$ vertices after adding the edge $(u_{k-1},u_0)$.
differentia: adding the edge $(u_{k-1},u_0)$

nodes.name: strongly connected digraph
nodes.statement: A digraph $\G$ is \emph{strongly connected} if for all $u,v \in V(\G)$ there is a directed path in $E(\G)$ from $u$ to $v$ (note that we take this to include the situation $u=v$, but for reflexive graphs the distinction is moot).
differentia: for all $u,v \in V(\G)$ there is a directed path in $E(\G)$ from $u$ to $v$

nodes.name: weakly connected digraph
nodes.statement: A digraph is \emph{weakly connected} if its symmetric closure (underlying undirected graph) is connected.
differentia: its symmetric closure (underlying undirected graph) is connected

nodes.name: double-edge
nodes.statement: A \emph{double-edge} in a digraph $\G$ consists in a pair of distinct vertices $u,v \in V(\G)$, so that $(u,v),(v,u) \in E(\G)$.
nodes.genus: a pair of distinct vertices $u,v \in V(\G)$

nodes.name: semicomplete digraph
nodes.statement: A digraph $\G$ is \emph{semicomplete} if for every two distinct vertices $u$ and $v$, at least one of $(u,v)$, $(v,u)$ belongs to $E(\G)$.
differentia: for every two distinct vertices $u$ and $v$, at least one of $(u,v)$, $(v,u)$ belongs to $E(\G)$

nodes.name: tournament
nodes.statement: A digraph~$\G$ is a \emph{tournament} if for every two distinct vertices $u$ and $v$, exactly one of $(u,v)$, $(v,u)$ belongs to $E(\G)$.
differentia: for every two distinct vertices $u$ and $v$, exactly one of $(u,v)$, $(v,u)$ belongs to $E(\G)$

nodes.name: transitive reflexive tournament
nodes.statement: A reflexive tournament $\G$ is \emph{transitive} if for every triple of vertices $u,v,w$ with $(u,v), (v,w)\in E(\G)$, also $(u,w)$ belongs to $E(\G)$.
differentia: for every triple of vertices $u,v,w$ with $(u,v), (v,w)\in E(\G)$, also $(u,w)$ belongs to $E(\G)$

nodes.name: subgraph / induced subgraph
nodes.statement: A digraph~$\F$ is a \emph{subgraph} of a digraph $\G$ if $V(\F) \subseteq V(\G)$ and $E(\F) \subseteq E(\G)$. It is \emph{induced} if $E(\F)$ coincides with $E(\G)$ restricted to pairs containing only vertices of $V(\F)$.
differentia: $V(\F) \subseteq V(\G)$ and $E(\F) \subseteq E(\G)$
$E(\F)$ coincides with $E(\G)$ restricted to pairs containing only vertices of $V(\F)$

nodes.name: subtournament
nodes.statement: A \emph{subtournament} is an induced subgraph of a tournament (note that this is a fortiori a tournament).
nodes.genus: an induced subgraph of a tournament

nodes.name: homomorphism of digraphs
nodes.statement: A \emph{homomorphism} from a digraph~$\G$ to a digraph~$\H$ is a function $f:V(\G)\rightarrow V(\H)$ so that for all $u,v \in V(\G)$ with $(u,v) \in E(\G)$ we have $(f(u),f(v)) \in E(\H)$.
differentia: for all $u,v \in V(\G)$ with $(u,v) \in E(\G)$ we have $(f(u),f(v)) \in E(\H)$

nodes.name: (vertex)-surjective homomorphism
nodes.statement: We say that $f$ is \emph{(vertex)-surjective} if for every vertex $x\in V(\H)$ there exists a vertex $u\in V(\G)$ with $f(u)=x$.
differentia: for every vertex $x\in V(\H)$ there exists a vertex $u\in V(\G)$ with $f(u)=x$

nodes.name: homomorphic image
nodes.statement: A \emph{homomorphic image} of $\H$ is a digraph $\H'$ so that there is a surjective homomorphism $h:\H \rightarrow \H'$ in which, for all $(x',y') \in E(\H')$ there exists $(x,y) \in E(\H)$ so that $x'=h(x)$ and $y'=h(y)$. That is, $h$ is vertex- and edge-surjective.
differentia: there is a surjective homomorphism $h:\H \rightarrow \H'$ in which, for all $(x',y') \in E(\H')$ there exists $(x,y) \in E(\H)$ so that $x'=h(x)$ and $y'=h(y)$

nodes.name: direct product of digraphs
nodes.statement: The \emph{direct product} of two digraphs $\G$ and $\H$, denoted $\G \times \H$, has vertex set $V(\G) \times V(\H)$ and edges $((x,y),(x',y'))$ exactly when $(x,x') \in E(\G)$ and $(y,y') \in E(\H)$. This product is associative and commutative, up to isomorphism, and spawns a natural power.
differentia: vertex set $V(\G) \times V(\H)$ and edges $((x,y),(x',y'))$ exactly when $(x,x') \in E(\G)$ and $(y,y') \in E(\H)$

nodes.name: $k$-ary polymorphism
nodes.statement: A $k$-ary \emph{polymorphism} of $\G$ is a function $f:\G^k\rightarrow \G$ so that when $(x_1,y_1),\ldots,$ $(x_k,y_k) \in E(\G)$ then $(f(x_1,\ldots,x_k),f(y_1,\ldots,y_k)) \in E(\G)$. A polymorphism of $\G$ can be seen as a homomorphism from the $k$th (direct) power of $\G$, $\G^k$, to $\G$.
nodes.statement_short: A $k$-ary operation on $V(\G)$ preserving $E(\G)$ coordinatewise; equivalently a homomorphism $\G^k \to \G$.
differentia: when $(x_1,y_1),\ldots,$ $(x_k,y_k) \in E(\G)$ then $(f(x_1,\ldots,x_k),f(y_1,\ldots,y_k)) \in E(\G)$

nodes.name: idempotent polymorphism
nodes.statement: A polymorphism $f$ is \emph{idempotent} if for all $x\in V(\G)$, $f(x,\ldots,x)=x$.
differentia: for all $x\in V(\G)$, $f(x,\ldots,x)=x$

nodes.name: projection $\pi^i_k$
nodes.statement: The $k$-ary $i$th \emph{projection}, for $i \in [k]$, is the polymorphism $\pi^i_k$ given by $\pi^i_k(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=x_i$.
differentia: $\pi^i_k(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=x_i$

nodes.name: essentially unary operation
nodes.statement: A $k$-ary operation $f$ is called \emph{essentially unary} if there exists a unary operation $g$ and $i \in [k]$ so that $f(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=g(x_i)$ for all $(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\in \G^k$.
nodes.statement_short: A $k$-ary operation that depends on only one of its arguments.
differentia: there exists a unary operation $g$ and $i \in [k]$ so that $f(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=g(x_i)$

nodes.name: endomorphism
nodes.statement: An \emph{endomorphism} of~$\G$ is a homomorphism from $\G$ to itself.

nodes.name: constant map
nodes.statement: An endomorphism~$e$ of $\G$ is a \emph{constant map} if there exists a vertex $v\in V(\G)$ such that $e(u)=v$ for all $u\in V(\G)$.
differentia: there exists a vertex $v\in V(\G)$ such that $e(u)=v$ for all $u\in V(\G)$

nodes.name: self-map digraph $\G^{\G}$
nodes.statement: The \emph{self-map digraph} $\G^{\G}$ has as its vertices the self-maps of $V(\G)$, and there is an edge $(f,g) \in E(\G^\G)$ between self-maps $f$ and $g$ if and only if for every edge $(x,y) \in E(\G)$, we have that $(f(x),g(y)) \in E(\G)$.
nodes.statement_short: The digraph on all self-maps of $V(\G)$ with $(f,g)$ an edge iff $f,g$ jointly preserve every edge of $\G$.
differentia: there is an edge $(f,g) \in E(\G^\G)$ between self-maps $f$ and $g$ if and only if for every edge $(x,y) \in E(\G)$, we have that $(f(x),g(y)) \in E(\G)$

nodes.name: endomorphism digraph $\widehat{\G^{\G}}$
nodes.statement: The \emph{endomorphism digraph} $\widehat{\G^{\G}}$ is the restriction of the self-map digraph $\G^{\G}$ to the vertices induced by endomorphisms of $\G$.
nodes.genus: the restriction of the self-map digraph $\G^{\G}$
differentia: to the vertices induced by endomorphisms of $\G$

nodes.name: Self-loops of $\G^{\G}$ are the endomorphisms
nodes.statement: Note that the self-loops of $\G^{\G}$ are precisely the endomorphisms of $\G$, so $\widehat{\G^{\G}}$ is reflexive when $\G$ is reflexive.
nodes.statement_short: The looped vertices of the self-map digraph are exactly the endomorphisms, so $\widehat{\G^{\G}}$ inherits reflexivity.
assumptions: when $\G$ is reflexive
conclusions: the self-loops of $\G^{\G}$ are precisely the endomorphisms of $\G$
$\widehat{\G^{\G}}$ is reflexive

nodes.name: Composition closure of edges in $\widehat{\G^\G}$
nodes.statement: If $(f_1,g_1) \in E(\widehat{\G^\G})$ and $(f_2,g_2) \in E(\widehat{\G^\G})$, then $((f_1 \circ f_2),(g_1 \circ g_2)) \in E(\widehat{\G^\G})$.
nodes.statement_short: Edges of the endomorphism digraph are closed under componentwise composition.
assumptions: $(f_1,g_1) \in E(\widehat{\G^\G})$ and $(f_2,g_2) \in E(\widehat{\G^\G})$
conclusions: $((f_1 \circ f_2),(g_1 \circ g_2)) \in E(\widehat{\G^\G})$

nodes.name: Currying a homomorphism $\H\times\G \to \G$ into $\H \to \widehat{\G^{\G}}$
nodes.statement: Let $\G$ and $\H$ be two digraphs. Let $\phi$ be a homomorphism from $\H\times \G$ to~$\G$. Then the function $\psi$ defined by $\psi(x)(u)=\phi(x,u)$ for all $x\in V(\H)$, $u\in V(\G)$ is a homomorphism from $\H$ to $\widehat{\G^{\G}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Currying turns a homomorphism $\H \times \G \to \G$ into a homomorphism $\H \to \widehat{\G^{\G}}$.
assumptions: Let $\G$ and $\H$ be two digraphs.
Let $\phi$ be a homomorphism from $\H\times \G$ to~$\G$.
conclusions: the function $\psi$ defined by $\psi(x)(u)=\phi(x,u)$ for all $x\in V(\H)$, $u\in V(\G)$ is a homomorphism from $\H$ to $\widehat{\G^{\G}}$

nodes.name: automorphism
nodes.statement: A bijective endomorphism whose inverse is a homomorphism is an \emph{automorphism}.
differentia: whose inverse is a homomorphism

nodes.name: non-trivial endomorphism
nodes.statement: An endomorphism is \emph{non-trivial} if it is neither an automorphism nor a constant map.
differentia: it is neither an automorphism nor a constant map

nodes.name: core
nodes.statement: A digraph, all of whose endomorphisms are automorphisms, is termed a \emph{core}.
differentia: all of whose endomorphisms are automorphisms

nodes.name: an endomorphism fixes a subset / subgraph (up to automorphism)
nodes.statement: An endomorphism $e$ of a digraph~$\H$ \emph{fixes} a subset $S \subseteq V(\H)$ if $e(S)=S$, that is, $e(x)\in S$ for all $x \in S$, and it fixes a subgraph~$\F$ of $\H$ if $e(\F)=\F$. It fixes an induced subgraph~$\F$ \emph{up to automorphism} if $e(\F)$ is an automorphic copy of $\F$ (this is a stronger condition than $e(\F)$ being isomorphic to $\F$).
nodes.statement_short: $e$ fixes $S$ when $e(S)=S$, and fixes $\F$ up to automorphism when $e(\F)$ is an automorphic copy of $\F$.
differentia: $e(S)=S$, that is, $e(x)\in S$ for all $x \in S$
$e(\F)$ is an automorphic copy of $\F$

nodes.name: retraction
nodes.statement: An endomorphism~$r$ of $\G$ is a \emph{retraction} of $\G$ if $r$ is the identity on the image $r(\G)$ (thus a retraction must have at least one fixed point).
differentia: $r$ is the identity on the image $r(\G)$

nodes.name: Tournaments have more than one vertex
nodes.statement: We demand our tournaments have more than one vertex (to rule out certain trivial cases in proofs).

nodes.name: All subgraphs considered are induced
nodes.statement: All subgraphs we consider in this paper will be induced.

nodes.name: endo-trivial digraph
nodes.statement: A digraph is \emph{endo-trivial} if all of its endomorphisms are automorphisms or constant maps.
differentia: all of its endomorphisms are automorphisms or constant maps

nodes.name: Endo-triviality equals minimality of the polymorphism algebra
nodes.statement: The concept of endo-triviality also arises from the perspective of the algebra of polymorphisms. An algebra is called minimal if its unary polynomials are either constants or the permutations (see Definition~2.14 in \cite{HobbyMcKenzie}). For reflexive digraphs, polynomials and polymorphisms coincide. In other words, a reflexive digraph is endo-trivial if and only if its associated algebra of polymorphisms is minimal.
nodes.statement_short: For reflexive digraphs, endo-triviality is exactly minimality of the associated polymorphism algebra.

nodes.name: retract-trivial digraph
nodes.statement: A digraph is \emph{retract-trivial} if all of its retractions are the identity or constant maps.
differentia: all of its retractions are the identity or constant maps

nodes.name: Retract-triviality equals term-minimality
nodes.statement: The concept of retract-triviality also appears in the algebraic theory but has, as far as we are aware, not been studied in a combinatorial setting. An algebra is term-minimal if the only retractions in its clone of terms are the identity and constants (see~\cite{TermMinimalAlgebras}). A reflexive digraph is retract-minimal if its associated algebra of polymorphisms is term-minimal. It follows that on reflexive digraphs, the concepts of retract-minimality and retract-triviality coincide.
nodes.statement_short: On reflexive digraphs retract-triviality coincides with term-minimality of the polymorphism clone; the notion is new combinatorially.

nodes.name: Endo-trivial implies retract-trivial (converse fails in general)
nodes.statement: We note that every endo-trivial structure is also retract-trivial. However, the reverse implication is not necessarily true: in Figure~\ref{fig:Tournament6} we give an example of a structure that is retract-trivial but not endo-trivial. This example is based on a digraph but is not itself a digraph. It is also possible to construct a retract-trivial digraph that is not endo-trivial~\cite{Si17}, but on reflexive tournaments both concepts do coincide.
nodes.statement_short: Endo-triviality implies retract-triviality, but not conversely in general.
assumptions: every endo-trivial structure
conclusions: is also retract-trivial
the reverse implication is not necessarily true

nodes.name: A six-vertex tournament yielding a retract-trivial, non-endo-trivial structure $\B$
nodes.statement: A tournament on six vertices (self-loops are not drawn), which retracts to the directed 3-cycle (in black) on the right-hand side, but not to the one on the left-hand side (in black as well). However, there is no endomorphism that maps the left-hand one isomorphically to the right. We can use this tournament to build a structure that is a counterexample to the generalisation of Lemma~\ref{lem:endo-retraction-trivial} stating that endo-trivial and retract-trivial coincide. Let us label the vertices in the tournament: $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ (left-hand $\DC^*_3$, clockwise from bottom) and $0,1,2$ (right-hand $\DC^*_3$, clockwise from bottom). Let us build a structure $\B$ by augmenting a new $6$-ary relation with tuples in $\{(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,0,1,2),(\alpha,\alpha,\alpha,\alpha,\beta,\gamma),(\alpha,\alpha,\alpha,\alpha,\alpha,\alpha)\}$. The structure~$\B$ is retract-trivial but is not endo-trivial, since it has an interesting endomorphism that takes $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,0,1,2)$ to $(\alpha,\alpha,\alpha,\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$.
nodes.statement_short: A 6-vertex tournament augmented by a $6$-ary relation gives a structure that is retract-trivial but not endo-trivial.

nodes.name: Endo-triviality and retract-triviality coincide on reflexive tournaments

nodes.name: Proof of the endo-trivial/retract-trivial equivalence for reflexive tournaments
nodes.statement: (Forwards.) Trivial. (Backwards.) By contraposition, suppose $e$ is a non-trivial endomorphism of a reflexive tournament $\H$. Consider $e(\H)$ and build some function $e^{-1}$ from $e(\H)$ to $\H$ by choosing $e^{-1}(y)=x$ if $e(x)=y$ arbitrarily. Since $\H$ is a (reflexive) tournament, $e^{-1}$ is an isomorphism, whereupon $e^{-1} \circ e$ is the identity automorphism when restricted to some subtournament $\H_0$ of $\H$. Hence $e^{-1} \circ e$ is a non-trivial retraction of $\H$ (to $\H_0$).
nodes.statement_short: Contrapositive: from a non-trivial endomorphism $e$ build a right inverse $e^{-1}$ and use $e^{-1}\circ e$ as a non-trivial retraction.

nodes.name: Forward direction

nodes.name: Backward direction by contraposition

Consider $e(\H)$ and build some function $e^{-1}$ from $e(\H)$ to $\H$ by choosing $e^{-1}(y)=x$ if $e(x)=y$ arbitrarily. nodes.statement_short: Build $e^{-1}$ on $e(\H)$; then $e^{-1}\circ e$ is a non-trivial retraction.

nodes.name: Proof of the structure lemma for retract-trivial reflexive digraphs
nodes.statement: (1) As any reflexive digraph can be retracted onto a double edge, the result follows. \\[3pt] (2) A reflexive digraph that is not weakly connected may be retracted onto a 2-vertex digraph. So we may safely assume $\H$ is weakly connected. If~$\H$ is not strongly connected, then $\H$ has an edge $(a,b)$ such that $a$ and $b$ are in different strong components, that is, there is no directed path from $b$ to $a$. We define a retraction of $\H$ onto the subgraph induced by $\{a,b\}$ as follows: let $r(x) = a$ if there exists a directed path from $x$ to $a$ and $r(x)=b$ otherwise. As $r(a)=a$ and $r(b)=b$, it remains to check if $r$ is an endomorphism. Let $(x,y)$ be an edge. If $r(y)=a$, then there exists a directed path from $y$ to~$a$, and thus a directed path from $x$ to~$a$ implying that $r(a)=a$. If $r(y)=b$, then $r(x)=a$ and $r(x)=b$ are both allowed.\\[3pt] (3) We first prove that no constant map is adjacent to an automorphism in $\widehat{\H^{\H}}$. Suppose for a contradiction that there exists an automorphism $\sigma$ backwards-adjacent to some constant (the case of forwards-adjacent is dual). Thus without loss of generality we may assume that $(\sigma,c) \in E(\widehat{\H^\H})$ for some constant map $c$, say for all $u\in V(\H)$, $c(u)=v$ for some $v\in V(\H)$. By composing sufficiently many times via Lemma~\ref{l-gg2}, we obtain that $(id_\H,c) \in E(\widehat{\H^\H})$. Since $\H$ is strongly connected, every vertex $u\in V(\H)$ has out-degree at least~1. Hence $(u,v) \in E(\H)$ for all $u \in V(\H)$. Since $v$ has out-degree at least~1, this means that $\H$ contains a double edge, contradicting statement~(1). Now suppose that there exists an automorphism $\sigma$ that is backward-adjacent to some endomorphism $f \neq \sigma$ (the case of forwards-adjacent is dual). Thus, without loss of generality we have $(\sigma,f) \in E(\widehat{\H^\H})$. Apply $\sigma^{-1}$ to both sides of the edge to obtain that $(id_\H,g) \in E(\widehat{\H^\H})$ for some $g \neq id_\H$. By the preceding lemma, and the fact that $\H$ is retract-trivial, this means $g$ is a constant map, contradicting the claim above.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
nodes.statement_short: Three retraction constructions: onto a double edge, onto a 2-vertex digraph across strong components, then a composition/contradiction argument for isolation of automorphisms.

nodes.name: Part (1): no double edge
nodes.statement: (1) As any reflexive digraph can be retracted onto a double edge, the result follows.

nodes.name: Part (2): strong connectivity
nodes.statement: (2) A reflexive digraph that is not weakly connected may be retracted onto a 2-vertex digraph. So we may safely assume $\H$ is weakly connected. If~$\H$ is not strongly connected, then $\H$ has an edge $(a,b)$ such that $a$ and $b$ are in different strong components, that is, there is no directed path from $b$ to $a$. nodes.name: Part (3a): no constant map is adjacent to an automorphism

Suppose for a contradiction that there exists an automorphism $\sigma$ backwards-adjacent to some constant (the case of forwards-adjacent is dual). Thus without loss of generality we may assume that $(\sigma,c) \in E(\widehat{\H^\H})$ for some constant map $c$, say for all $u\in V(\H)$, $c(u)=v$ for some $v\in V(\H)$. Hence $(u,v) \in E(\H)$ for all $u \in V(\H)$. Since $v$ has out-degree at least~1, this means that $\H$ contains a double edge, contradicting statement~(1).

nodes.statement_short: Composing an automorphism-to-constant edge yields $(id_\H,c)$, forcing a double edge, contradicting (1).

nodes.name: Part (3b): automorphisms are isolated
nodes.statement: Now suppose that there exists an automorphism $\sigma$ that is backward-adjacent to some endomorphism $f \neq \sigma$ (the case of forwards-adjacent is dual). Thus, without loss of generality we have $(\sigma,f) \in E(\widehat{\H^\H})$. Apply $\sigma^{-1}$ to both sides of the edge to obtain that $(id_\H,g) \in E(\widehat{\H^\H})$ for some $g \neq id_\H$. By the preceding lemma, and the fact that $\H$ is retract-trivial, this means $g$ is a constant map, contradicting the claim above.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
nodes.statement_short: Translate any edge at $\sigma$ to an edge at $id_\H$ and apply the Maroti-Zadori lemma to reach a contradiction.

nodes.name: Endo-trivial reflexive digraphs have only essentially unary polymorphisms
nodes.statement: Let $\H$ be an endo-trivial reflexive digraph with at least three vertices. Then every polymorphism of $\H$ is essentially unary.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
nodes.statement_short: Every polymorphism of an endo-trivial reflexive digraph on $\ge 3$ vertices depends on a single variable.
assumptions: Let $\H$ be an endo-trivial reflexive digraph with at least three vertices.
conclusions: every polymorphism of $\H$ is essentially unary

nodes.name: Proof that endo-triviality forces essential unarity
nodes.statement: Since $\H$ is endo-trivial, $\H$ is retract-trivial. Hence, by Lemma~\ref{lem:Benoit-lemma}, $\H$ is strongly connected, and furthermore the automorphisms of $\H$ are isolated vertices of~$\widehat{\H^{\H}}$. As $\H$ is endo-trivial, this means that $\widehat{\H^{\H}}$ is the disjoint union of a copy of $\H$ that corresponds to the constant maps and a set of isolated vertices, one for each automorphism of $\H$. Suppose for a contradiction that there exists an an $n$-ary polymorphism~$f$ of $\H$ which is not essentially unary. We may without loss of generality assume that~$f$ depends on all of its $n$ variables, where $n \geq 2$. By Lemma~\ref{l-gg3}, the mapping $F:\H^{n-1} \rightarrow \widehat{\H^{\H}}$ defined by $F(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1})(y) = f(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1},y)$ is a homomorphism. Since $\H$ is strongly connected, so is $\H^{n-1}$, and hence so is the image of $F$ in $\widehat{\H^{\H}}$. Thus this image is either contained in the component of constants, in which case $f$ does not depend on its last variable, else it is a singleton, in which case $f$ does not depend on any of its first $n-1$ variables.

nodes.statement_short: Curry a hypothetical non-essentially-unary polymorphism into a homomorphism $\H^{n-1} \to \widehat{\H^{\H}}$ and use connectivity of the image to force degeneracy.

nodes.name: Decompose the endomorphism digraph
nodes.statement: Since $\H$ is endo-trivial, $\H$ is retract-trivial. Hence, by Lemma~\ref{lem:Benoit-lemma}, $\H$ is strongly connected, and furthermore the automorphisms of $\H$ are isolated vertices of~$\widehat{\H^{\H}}$. As $\H$ is endo-trivial, this means that $\widehat{\H^{\H}}$ is the disjoint union of a copy of $\H$ that corresponds to the constant maps and a set of isolated vertices, one for each automorphism of $\H$.

nodes.statement_short: $\widehat{\H^{\H}}$ splits into a copy of $\H$ (the constants) plus isolated automorphisms.

nodes.name: Assume a non-essentially-unary polymorphism
nodes.statement: Suppose for a contradiction that there exists an an $n$-ary polymorphism~$f$ of $\H$ which is not essentially unary. We may without loss of generality assume that~$f$ depends on all of its $n$ variables, where $n \geq 2$.

nodes.statement_short: Take $f$ depending on all $n \ge 2$ of its variables.

nodes.name: Curry $f$ into a homomorphism into $\widehat{\H^{\H}}$
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{l-gg3}, the mapping $F:\H^{n-1} \rightarrow \widehat{\H^{\H}}$ defined by $F(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1})(y) = f(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1},y)$ is a homomorphism. Since $\H$ is strongly connected, so is $\H^{n-1}$, and hence so is the image of $F$ in $\widehat{\H^{\H}}$.

nodes.statement_short: Apply the currying lemma; strong connectivity of $\H^{n-1}$ transfers to the image.

nodes.name: Both possible images force degeneracy
nodes.statement: Thus this image is either contained in the component of constants, in which case $f$ does not depend on its last variable, else it is a singleton, in which case $f$ does not depend on any of its first $n-1$ variables.

assumptions: If $\H$ is a reflexive tournament that is endo-trivial
conclusions: $\H$ contains a directed Hamilton cycle

any homomorphic image of $\H$ of size $1<n<|V(\H)|$

nodes.name: Proof that intermediate homomorphic images carry a double edge
nodes.statement: Suppose $\H$ has a homomorphic image of size $1<n<|V(\H)|$ without a double edge. By looking at the equivalence classes of vertices identified in the homomorphic image, we can deduce a non-trivial retraction, namely by mapping each of the vertices in an equivalence class to any particular one of them.

nodes.name: the gadget $\Cylm$
nodes.statement: We now introduce the gadget $\Cylm$ drawn in Figure~\ref{fig:Photo2}. We take $m$ disjoint copies of the directed $m$-cycle $\DCm$ arranged in a cylindrical fashion so that there is an edge from $i$ in the $j$th copy to $i$ in the $j+1$th copy (drawn in red), and an edge from $i$ in the $j+1$th copy to $i+1$ in the $j$th copy (drawn in green). We consider $\DCm$ to have vertices $\{1,\ldots,m\}$.
nodes.statement_short: $m$ cylindrically stacked copies of the directed $m$-cycle $\DCm$, joined by red $i\to i$ and green $i\to i+1$ edges between consecutive copies.
differentia: arranged in a cylindrical fashion so that there is an edge from $i$ in the $j$th copy to $i$ in the $j+1$th copy (drawn in red), and an edge from $i$ in the $j+1$th copy to $i+1$ in the $j$th copy (drawn in green)

nodes.name: the Hamilton cycle $\HC_m$ attached to the gadget
nodes.statement: A key role will be played by Hamilton cycles $\HC_m$ in a strongly connected reflexive tournament on $m$ vertices. We consider this cycle also labelled $\{1,\ldots,m\}$, in order to attach it to the gadget $\Cylm$.
nodes.genus: Hamilton cycles $\HC_m$ in a strongly connected reflexive tournament on $m$ vertices

nodes.name: Provenance of the gadget $\Cylm$
nodes.statement: The gadget $\Cylm$ is an alteration of a gadget that appears in \cite{FederHell98} for proving that {\sc List $\H$-Colouring} is \NP-complete when $\H$ is an undirected cycle on at least four vertices, but our proof is very different.

nodes.name: Collapsing the bottom cycle collapses the whole gadget
nodes.statement: In any homomorphism $h$ from $\Cylm$, with bottom cycle $\DCm$, to a reflexive tournament, if $|h(\DCm)|=1$, then $|h(\Cylm)|=1$.
nodes.statement_short: If a homomorphism of $\Cylm$ into a reflexive tournament collapses the bottom cycle, it collapses everything.
assumptions: In any homomorphism $h$ from $\Cylm$, with bottom cycle $\DCm$, to a reflexive tournament
if $|h(\DCm)|=1$

nodes.name: Property $(\dagger)$ of the gadget $\Cylm$
nodes.statement: We will use another property, denoted \textbf{$(\dagger)$}, of $\Cylm$, which is that the retractions from $\Cylm$ to its bottom copy of $\DCm$, once propagated through the intermediate copies, induce on the top copy precisely the set of automorphisms of $\DCm$. That is, the top copy of $\DCm$ is mapped isomorphically to the bottom copy, and all such isomorphisms may be realised. The reason is that in such a retraction, the $(j+1)$th copy may either map under the identity to the $j$th copy, or rotate one edge of the cycle clockwise, and $\Cylm$ consists of sufficiently many (namely $m$) copies of $\DCm$.
nodes.statement_short: Retractions of $\Cylm$ onto its bottom $\DCm$ realise exactly the automorphisms of $\DCm$ on the top copy.
assumptions: the retractions from $\Cylm$ to its bottom copy of $\DCm$, once propagated through the intermediate copies
conclusions: induce on the top copy precisely the set of automorphisms of $\DCm$

nodes.name: $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H_0,\HC_0])$
nodes.statement: Now let $\H$ be a reflexive tournament that contains a subtournament~$\H_0$ on $m$ vertices that is endo-trivial. By Lemma~\ref{l-Ham}, we find that $\H_0$ contains at least one directed Hamilton cycle $\HC_0$. Define $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H_0,\HC_0])$ as follows. Begin with $\H$ and add a copy of the gadget $\Cylm$, where the bottom copy of $\DCm$ is identified with $\HC_0$, to build a digraph~$\F(\H_0,\HC_0)$. Now ask, for some $y \in V(\H)$ whether there is a retraction $r$ of $\F(\H_0,\HC_0)$ to $\H$ so that some vertex $x$ in the top copy of $\DCm$ in $\Cylm$ is such that $r(x)=y$. Such vertices $y$ comprise the set $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H_0,\HC_0])$.
nodes.statement_short: The set of vertices of $\H$ reachable as the image of a top-copy gadget vertex under some retraction of $\F(\H_0,\HC_0)$ to $\H$.
differentia: there is a retraction $r$ of $\F(\H_0,\HC_0)$ to $\H$ so that some vertex $x$ in the top copy of $\DCm$ in $\Cylm$ is such that $r(x)=y$

nodes.name: Remark 1: spill can always be witnessed on the top copy
nodes.statement: If $x$ belongs to some copy of $\DCm$ that is not the top copy, we can find a vertex~$x'$ in the top copy of $\DCm$ and a retraction $r'$ from $\F(\H_0,\HC_0)$ to $\H$ with $r'(x')=r(x)=y$, namely by letting $r'$ map the vertices of higher copies of~$\DCm$ to the image of their corresponding vertex in the copy that contains~$x$. In particular this implies that $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H_0,\HC_0])$ contains $V(\H_0)$.
nodes.statement_short: A witness in any copy of $\DCm$ can be pushed to the top copy, so the spill set always contains $V(\H_0)$.

nodes.name: Full spillage when $\H$ retracts to $\H_0$
nodes.statement: If $\H$ is a reflexive tournament that retracts to a subtournament~$\H_0$ with Hamilton cycle~$\HC_0$, then $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H_0,\HC_0])=V(\H)$.
assumptions: If $\H$ is a reflexive tournament that retracts to a subtournament~$\H_0$ with Hamilton cycle~$\HC_0$
conclusions: $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H_0,\HC_0])=V(\H)$

nodes.name: Proof of full spillage
nodes.statement: let $y \in V(\H) \setminus V(\H_0)$. We need to prove that there exists a retraction~$r$ from $\F(\H_0,\HC_0)$ to $\H$ with $r(x)=y$ for some vertex~$x$ in the top copy of $\DCm$ in $\Cylm$. Let $h$ be a retraction of $\H$ to $\H_0$. Suppose $h(y)=i$. We observe that both $(i-1,y)$ and $(y,i+1)$ are edges of $E(\H)$. However, we might have either $(y,i)$ or $(i,y)$ and distinguish between these two cases. First suppose that $(y,i) \in E(\H)$. Then we retract the gadget $\Cylm$ associated with $y$ in the following fashion. Using property $(\dagger)$ we turn successive copies of $\DCm$ in such a way as necessary to ensure that the vertex directly below $y$ is at position $i$; for a diagrammatic description of what means ``below'', see Figure~\ref{fig:Photo2}. Ih the top copy of $\DCm$ we map the $i$th vertex to $y$ and the $j$th vertex ($j\neq i$) to $j$ in $\H_0$. Now suppose that $(i,y) \in E(\H)$.) Then we retract the gadget $\Cylm$ associated with $y$ in the following fashion. Using property $(\dagger)$ we turn successive copies of $\DCm$ in such a way as necessary to ensure that the vertex directly below $y$ is at position $i-1$; wherein with the last copy of $\DCm$ we map the $i$th vertex to $y$ and the $j$th vertex ($j\neq i$) to $j$ in $\H_0$. Note that, in both cases, all of the vertices of $\Cylm$, except one, are mapped to $\H_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Rotate the gadget copies via property $(\dagger)$ so that $y$ sits above position $i$ or $i-1$, splitting on whether $(y,i)$ or $(i,y)$ is an edge.

nodes.name: Set up the retraction and the two cases
nodes.statement: let $y \in V(\H) \setminus V(\H_0)$. We need to prove that there exists a retraction~$r$ from $\F(\H_0,\HC_0)$ to $\H$ with $r(x)=y$ for some vertex~$x$ in the top copy of $\DCm$ in $\Cylm$. Let $h$ be a retraction of $\H$ to $\H_0$. Suppose $h(y)=i$. We observe that both $(i-1,y)$ and $(y,i+1)$ are edges of $E(\H)$. However, we might have either $(y,i)$ or $(i,y)$ and distinguish between these two cases.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $y$ outside $\H_0$, let $h(y)=i$, and split on the direction of the edge between $y$ and $i$.

nodes.name: Case $(y,i) \in E(\H)$
nodes.statement: First suppose that $(y,i) \in E(\H)$. Then we retract the gadget $\Cylm$ associated with $y$ in the following fashion. Using property $(\dagger)$ we turn successive copies of $\DCm$ in such a way as necessary to ensure that the vertex directly below $y$ is at position $i$; for a diagrammatic description of what means ``below'', see Figure~\ref{fig:Photo2}. Ih the top copy of $\DCm$ we map the $i$th vertex to $y$ and the $j$th vertex ($j\neq i$) to $j$ in $\H_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Rotate copies so the vertex below $y$ is at position $i$, then map the top copy accordingly.

nodes.name: Case $(i,y) \in E(\H)$
nodes.statement: Now suppose that $(i,y) \in E(\H)$.) Then we retract the gadget $\Cylm$ associated with $y$ in the following fashion. Using property $(\dagger)$ we turn successive copies of $\DCm$ in such a way as necessary to ensure that the vertex directly below $y$ is at position $i-1$; wherein with the last copy of $\DCm$ we map the $i$th vertex to $y$ and the $j$th vertex ($j\neq i$) to $j$ in $\H_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Rotate instead to position $i-1$ and map the last copy accordingly.

nodes.name: Reunion of the cases
nodes.statement: Note that, in both cases, all of the vertices of $\Cylm$, except one, are mapped to $\H_0$.
nodes.statement_short: In both cases only one gadget vertex escapes $\H_0$.

nodes.name: Base Case I
nodes.statement: Let $\H$ be a reflexive tournament that retracts to an endo-trivial subtournament $\H_0$ with Hamilton cycle $\HC_0$. Assume that $\H$ retracts to $\H'_0$ for every isomorphic copy $\H'_0=i(\H_0)$ of $\H_0$ in $\H$ with $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H'_0,i(\HC_0)])=V(\H)$. Then $\H_0$-{\sc Retraction} can be polynomially reduced to {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring}.
nodes.statement_short: If $\H$ retracts onto an endo-trivial $\H_0$ and onto every full-spill isomorphic copy of it, then $\H_0$-Retraction reduces to Surjective $\H$-Colouring.
assumptions: Let $\H$ be a reflexive tournament that retracts to an endo-trivial subtournament $\H_0$ with Hamilton cycle $\HC_0$.
Assume that $\H$ retracts to $\H'_0$ for every isomorphic copy $\H'_0=i(\H_0)$ of $\H_0$ in $\H$ with $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H'_0,i(\HC_0)])=V(\H)$.
conclusions: $\H_0$-{\sc Retraction} can be polynomially reduced to {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring}

nodes.name: Proof of Base Case I
nodes.statement: Let $\G$ be an instance of $\H_0$-{\sc Retraction}. We build an instance~$\G''$ of {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring} in the following fashion. First, take a copy of $\H$ together with $\G$ and build $\G'$ by identifying these on the copy of $\H_0$ that they both possess as a subgraph. Let $m$ be the size of $\H_0$ and consider its Hamilton cycle $\HC_0$. We build $\G''$ from $\G'$ by augmenting a new copy of $\Cylm$ for every vertex $v \in V(\G') \setminus V(\H_0)$. Vertex~$v$ is to be identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\DCm$ in $\Cylm$ and the bottom copy of $\DCm$ is to be identified with $\HC_0$ in $\H_0$ according to the identity function. See Figure~\ref{f-new} for an example. We claim that $\G$ retracts to $\H_0$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\G''$ to $\H$. First suppose that $\G$ retracts to $\H_0$. Let $h$ be a retraction from $\G$ to $\H_0$. We extend $h$ as follows. First we map the copy of $\H$ in $\G''$ to itself in $\H$ by the identity. This will ensure surjectivity. We then map the various copies of $\Cylm$ in $\G''$. This is always possible: because $\H$ retracts to $\H_0$, we have $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H_0,\HC_0])=V(\H)$ due to Lemma~\ref{lem:spillage}. Hence, if $h(x)=y$ for two vertices $x\in V(\G')\setminus V(\H_0)$ and $y\in V(\H)$, we can always find a retraction of the graph $\F(\H_0,\HC_0)$ to $\H$ that maps $x$ to $y$, and we mimic this retraction on the corresponding subgraph in $\G''$. The crucial observation is that this can be done independently for each vertex in $V(\G')\setminus V(\H_0)$, as two vertices of different copies of $\Cylm$ are only adjacent if they both belong to $\G'$. This leads to a surjective homomorphism from $\G''$ to $\H$. Now suppose that there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\G''$ to $\H$. If $|h(\H_0)|=1$, then by Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1}, $|h(\Cylm)|=1$ for all copies of $\Cylm$ in $\G''$. This means that $|h(\G'')|=1$ and $h$ is not surjective, a contradiction. Now, $1<|h(\H_0)|<m$ is not possible either due to Lemma~\ref{lem:under-m}. Thus, $|h(\H_0)|=m$ and indeed $h$ maps $\H_0$ to a copy of itself in $\H$ which we will call $\H'_0=i(\H_0)$ for some isomorphism~$i$. We claim that $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H'_0,i(\HC_0)]) = V(\H)$. In order to see this, consider a vertex $y\in V(\H)$. As $h$ is surjective, there exists a vertex~$x\in V(\G'')$ with $h(x)=y$. By construction, $x$ belongs to some copy of $\DCm$, and thus also belongs to some copy of $\DCm$ in $\F(\H_0,\HC_0)$. We can extend $i^{-1}$ to an isomorphism from the copy of $\Cylm$ (which has $i(\HC_0)$ as its bottom cycle) in the graph $\F(\H_0',i(\HC_0))$ to the copy of $\Cylm$ (which has $\HC_0$ as its bottom cycle) in the graph $\F(\H_0,\HC_0)$. We define a mapping~$r^*$ from $\F(\H_0',i(\HC_0))$ to $\H$ by $r^*(u)=h\circ i^{-1}(u)$ if $u$ is on the copy of $\Cylm$ in $\F(\H_0',i(\HC_0))$ and $r^*(u)=u$ otherwise. We observe that $r^*(u)=u$ if $u\in V(\H_0')$ as $h$ coincides with $i$ on $\H_0$. As $\H_0$ separates the other vertices of the copy of $\Cylm$ from $V(\H)\setminus V(\H_0)$, in the sense that removing $\H_0$ would disconnect them, this means that $r^*$ is a retraction from $\F(\H_0',i(\HC_0))$ to $\H$. We find that $r^*$ maps $i(x)$ to $h\circ i^{-1}(i(x))=h(x)=y$. Moreover, as $x$ is in some copy of $\DCm$ in $\F(\H_0,\HC_0)$, we have that $i(x)$ is in some copy of $\DCm$ in $\F(\H'_0,i(\HC_0))$. We may assume without loss of generality that $i(x)$ belongs to the top copy (cf. Remark~1). We conclude that $y$ always belongs to $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H'_0,i(\HC_0)])$ (cf. Remark~1). As $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H'_0,i(\HC_0)]) = V(\H)$, we find, by assumption of the lemma, that there exists a retraction $r$ from $\H$ to $\H'_0$. Now $i^{-1} \circ r \circ h$ ia the desired retraction of $\G$ to~$\H_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Glue $\H$ to $\G$ along $\H_0$, hang a $\Cylm$ gadget on every outside vertex, and show the retraction and the surjective homomorphism correspond.

nodes.name: Construct the instance $\G''$
nodes.statement: Let $\G$ be an instance of $\H_0$-{\sc Retraction}. We build an instance~$\G''$ of {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring} in the following fashion. First, take a copy of $\H$ together with $\G$ and build $\G'$ by identifying these on the copy of $\H_0$ that they both possess as a subgraph. Let $m$ be the size of $\H_0$ and consider its Hamilton cycle $\HC_0$. We build $\G''$ from $\G'$ by augmenting a new copy of $\Cylm$ for every vertex $v \in V(\G') \setminus V(\H_0)$. Vertex~$v$ is to be identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\DCm$ in $\Cylm$ and the bottom copy of $\DCm$ is to be identified with $\HC_0$ in $\H_0$ according to the identity function. See Figure~\ref{f-new} for an example. We claim that $\G$ retracts to $\H_0$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\G''$ to $\H$.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $\H$ and $\G$ along $\H_0$ and attach one $\Cylm$ per outside vertex.

nodes.name: Forward direction: retraction gives a surjective homomorphism
nodes.statement: First suppose that $\G$ retracts to $\H_0$. Let $h$ be a retraction from $\G$ to $\H_0$. We extend $h$ as follows. First we map the copy of $\H$ in $\G''$ to itself in $\H$ by the identity. This will ensure surjectivity. We then map the various copies of $\Cylm$ in $\G''$. This is always possible: because $\H$ retracts to $\H_0$, we have $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H_0,\HC_0])=V(\H)$ due to Lemma~\ref{lem:spillage}. Hence, if $h(x)=y$ for two vertices $x\in V(\G')\setminus V(\H_0)$ and $y\in V(\H)$, we can always find a retraction of the graph $\F(\H_0,\HC_0)$ to $\H$ that maps $x$ to $y$, and we mimic this retraction on the corresponding subgraph in $\G''$. The crucial observation is that this can be done independently for each vertex in $V(\G')\setminus V(\H_0)$, as two vertices of different copies of $\Cylm$ are only adjacent if they both belong to $\G'$. This leads to a surjective homomorphism from $\G''$ to $\H$.
nodes.statement_short: Extend the retraction by the identity on $\H$ and by spill-realising maps on each gadget copy.

nodes.name: Backward direction: $h$ cannot collapse $\H_0$
nodes.statement: Now suppose that there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\G''$ to $\H$. If $|h(\H_0)|=1$, then by Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1}, $|h(\Cylm)|=1$ for all copies of $\Cylm$ in $\G''$. This means that $|h(\G'')|=1$ and $h$ is not surjective, a contradiction. Now, $1<|h(\H_0)|<m$ is not possible either due to Lemma~\ref{lem:under-m}. Thus, $|h(\H_0)|=m$ and indeed $h$ maps $\H_0$ to a copy of itself in $\H$ which we will call $\H'_0=i(\H_0)$ for some isomorphism~$i$.
nodes.statement_short: Rule out $|h(\H_0)|=1$ and $1<|h(\H_0)|<m$, so $h$ embeds $\H_0$ isomorphically.

nodes.name: The image copy has full spill
nodes.statement: We claim that $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H'_0,i(\HC_0)]) = V(\H)$. In order to see this, consider a vertex $y\in V(\H)$. As $h$ is surjective, there exists a vertex~$x\in V(\G'')$ with $h(x)=y$. By construction, $x$ belongs to some copy of $\DCm$, and thus also belongs to some copy of $\DCm$ in $\F(\H_0,\HC_0)$. We can extend $i^{-1}$ to an isomorphism from the copy of $\Cylm$ (which has $i(\HC_0)$ as its bottom cycle) in the graph $\F(\H_0',i(\HC_0))$ to the copy of $\Cylm$ (which has $\HC_0$ as its bottom cycle) in the graph $\F(\H_0,\HC_0)$. We define a mapping~$r^*$ from $\F(\H_0',i(\HC_0))$ to $\H$ by $r^*(u)=h\circ i^{-1}(u)$ if $u$ is on the copy of $\Cylm$ in $\F(\H_0',i(\HC_0))$ and $r^*(u)=u$ otherwise. We observe that $r^*(u)=u$ if $u\in V(\H_0')$ as $h$ coincides with $i$ on $\H_0$. As $\H_0$ separates the other vertices of the copy of $\Cylm$ from $V(\H)\setminus V(\H_0)$, in the sense that removing $\H_0$ would disconnect them, this means that $r^*$ is a retraction from $\F(\H_0',i(\HC_0))$ to $\H$. We find that $r^*$ maps $i(x)$ to $h\circ i^{-1}(i(x))=h(x)=y$. Moreover, as $x$ is in some copy of $\DCm$ in $\F(\H_0,\HC_0)$, we have that $i(x)$ is in some copy of $\DCm$ in $\F(\H'_0,i(\HC_0))$. We may assume without loss of generality that $i(x)$ belongs to the top copy (cf. Remark~1). We conclude that $y$ always belongs to $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H'_0,i(\HC_0)])$ (cf. Remark~1).
nodes.statement_short: Transport $h$ through $i^{-1}$ to build a retraction witnessing every $y \in V(\H)$ in the spill set.

nodes.name: Recover the retraction of $\G$ to $\H_0$
nodes.statement: As $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H'_0,i(\HC_0)]) = V(\H)$, we find, by assumption of the lemma, that there exists a retraction $r$ from $\H$ to $\H'_0$. Now $i^{-1} \circ r \circ h$ ia the desired retraction of $\G$ to~$\H_0$.
nodes.statement_short: The lemma's hypothesis gives a retraction $r$ onto $\H'_0$; then $i^{-1}\circ r\circ h$ works.

nodes.name: A six-vertex tournament with full spill but no retraction onto $\DC^*_3$
nodes.statement: An interesting tournament $\H$ on six vertices (self-loops are not drawn). This tournament does not retract to the $\DC^*_3$ on the left-hand side, yet $\mathrm{Spill}_3(\H[\DC^*_3,\DC_3]) = V(\H)$.
nodes.statement_short: A tournament whose spill set is everything although it does not retract to the relevant $\DC^*_3$ copy.

nodes.name: Endomorphisms mapping $\H_0$ to an isomorphic copy are automorphisms
nodes.statement: Let $\H$ be a reflexive tournament, containing a subtournament $\H_0$ so that any endomorphism of $\H$ that fixes $\H_0$ is an automorphism. Then any endomorphism of $\H$ that maps $\H_0$ to an isomorphic copy $\H'_0=i(\H_0)$ of itself is an automorphism of $\H$.
nodes.statement_short: If every $\H_0$-fixing endomorphism of $\H$ is an automorphism, so is every endomorphism sending $\H_0$ to an isomorphic copy.
assumptions: Let $\H$ be a reflexive tournament, containing a subtournament $\H_0$ so that any endomorphism of $\H$ that fixes $\H_0$ is an automorphism.
conclusions: any endomorphism of $\H$ that maps $\H_0$ to an isomorphic copy $\H'_0=i(\H_0)$ of itself is an automorphism of $\H$

nodes.name: Proof that $\H_0$-copy-preserving endomorphisms are automorphisms
nodes.statement: For contradiction, suppose there is an endomorphism $h$ that maps $\H_0$ to an isomorphic copy $\H'_0=i(\H_0)$ of itself that is not an automorphism of $\H$. In particular, $|h(\H)|<|V(\H)|$. Choose $h^{-1}$ in the following fashion. We let $h^{-1}$ of $h(\H_0)$ be the natural isomorphism of $h(\H_0)$ to $\H_0$ (that inverts the isomorphism given by $h$ from $\H_0$ to $\H'_0$). Otherwise we choose $h^{-1}$ arbitrarily, such that $h^{-1}(y)=x$ only if $h(x)=y$. Since $\H$ is a reflexive tournament, containing precisely one edge between distinct vertices, $h^{-1}$ is an isomorphism. Moreover, $h^{-1} \circ h$ is an endomorphism of $\H$ that fixes $\H_0$ and that is not an automorphism, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Build a right inverse $h^{-1}$ from tournament rigidity; $h^{-1}\circ h$ then fixes $\H_0$ without being an automorphism.

nodes.name: Set up the contradiction
nodes.statement: For contradiction, suppose there is an endomorphism $h$ that maps $\H_0$ to an isomorphic copy $\H'_0=i(\H_0)$ of itself that is not an automorphism of $\H$. In particular, $|h(\H)|<|V(\H)|$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume such an $h$ exists; then its image is proper.

nodes.name: Construct the inverse map $h^{-1}$
nodes.statement: Choose $h^{-1}$ in the following fashion. We let $h^{-1}$ of $h(\H_0)$ be the natural isomorphism of $h(\H_0)$ to $\H_0$ (that inverts the isomorphism given by $h$ from $\H_0$ to $\H'_0$). Otherwise we choose $h^{-1}$ arbitrarily, such that $h^{-1}(y)=x$ only if $h(x)=y$. Since $\H$ is a reflexive tournament, containing precisely one edge between distinct vertices, $h^{-1}$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Invert $h$ on $\H_0$ naturally and arbitrarily elsewhere; rigidity of reflexive tournaments makes it an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Derive the contradiction
nodes.statement: Moreover, $h^{-1} \circ h$ is an endomorphism of $\H$ that fixes $\H_0$ and that is not an automorphism, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: $h^{-1}\circ h$ fixes $\H_0$ but is not an automorphism, contradicting the hypothesis.

nodes.name: endo-trivial pair $(\H,\H_0)$
nodes.statement: Let $\H_0$ be an induced subgraph of a digraph $\H$. We say that the pair $(\H,\H_0)$ is \emph{endo-trivial} if all endomorphisms of $\H$ that fix $\H_0$ are automorphisms.
differentia: all endomorphisms of $\H$ that fix $\H_0$ are automorphisms

nodes.name: Base Case II
nodes.statement: Let $\H$ be a reflexive tournament with a subtournament~$\H_0$ with Hamilton cycle $\HC_0$ so that $(\H,\H_0)$ and $\H_0$ are endo-trivial and $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H_0,\HC_0]) = V(\H)$. Then $\H$-{\sc Retraction} can be polynomially reduced to {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring}.
nodes.statement_short: Under pairwise endo-triviality and full spill, $\H$-Retraction reduces to Surjective $\H$-Colouring.
assumptions: Let $\H$ be a reflexive tournament with a subtournament~$\H_0$ with Hamilton cycle $\HC_0$ so that $(\H,\H_0)$ and $\H_0$ are endo-trivial and $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H_0,\HC_0]) = V(\H)$.
conclusions: $\H$-{\sc Retraction} can be polynomially reduced to {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring}

nodes.name: Proof of Base Case II
nodes.statement: Let $\G$ be an instance of {\sc $\H$-Retraction}. We build an instance $\G'$ of {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring} in the following fashion. First we build $\G'$ from $\G$ by augmenting a new copy of $\Cylm$ for every vertex $v \in V(\G) \setminus V(\H_0)$. Vertex~$v$ is to be identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\DCm$ in $\Cylm$ and the bottom copy of $\DCm$ is to be identified with $\HC_0$ in $\H_0$ according to the identity function. We claim that $\G$ retracts to $\H$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\G'$ to $\H$. First suppose $\G$ retracts to $\H$. Let $r$ be a retraction from $\G$ to $\H$. Then any extension of~$r$ from $\G$ to $\G'$ is surjective. As $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H_0,\HC_0]) = V(\H)$ and two vertices in different copies of $\Cylm$ are only adjacent if both of them are in $\G$, we can in fact extend $r$ to a surjective homomorphism from $\G'$ to $\H$. Now suppose there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\G'$ to $\H$. If $|h(\H_0)|=1$, then Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1} tells us that $|h(\Cylm)|=1$ for all copies of $\Cylm$ in $\G'$, and then we derive $|h(\G')|=1$, contradicting the surjectivity of~$h$. Moreover, $1<|h(\H_0)|<m$ is not possible either due to Lemma~\ref{lem:under-m}. Thus, $|h(\H_0)|=m$ and $h$ maps $\H_0$ to a copy of itself. As $(\H,\H_0)$ is endo-trivial, Lemma~\ref{lem:7} tells us that the restriction of $h$ to $\H$ is an automorphism of $\H$, which we call $\alpha$. The required retraction from $\G$ to $\H$ is now given by $\alpha^{-1} \circ h$.
nodes.statement_short: Attach a $\Cylm$ gadget to each vertex outside $\H_0$; surjectivity then forces $h$ to restrict to an automorphism $\alpha$ of $\H$.

nodes.name: Construct the instance $\G'$
nodes.statement: Let $\G$ be an instance of {\sc $\H$-Retraction}. We build an instance $\G'$ of {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring} in the following fashion. First we build $\G'$ from $\G$ by augmenting a new copy of $\Cylm$ for every vertex $v \in V(\G) \setminus V(\H_0)$. Vertex~$v$ is to be identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\DCm$ in $\Cylm$ and the bottom copy of $\DCm$ is to be identified with $\HC_0$ in $\H_0$ according to the identity function. We claim that $\G$ retracts to $\H$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\G'$ to $\H$.
nodes.statement_short: Augment $\G$ with one $\Cylm$ per vertex outside $\H_0$.

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: First suppose $\G$ retracts to $\H$. Let $r$ be a retraction from $\G$ to $\H$. Then any extension of~$r$ from $\G$ to $\G'$ is surjective. As $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H_0,\HC_0]) = V(\H)$ and two vertices in different copies of $\Cylm$ are only adjacent if both of them are in $\G$, we can in fact extend $r$ to a surjective homomorphism from $\G'$ to $\H$.
nodes.statement_short: Full spill lets any retraction of $\G$ extend surjectively over the gadgets.

nodes.name: Backward direction via endo-triviality of the pair
nodes.statement: Now suppose there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\G'$ to $\H$. If $|h(\H_0)|=1$, then Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1} tells us that $|h(\Cylm)|=1$ for all copies of $\Cylm$ in $\G'$, and then we derive $|h(\G')|=1$, contradicting the surjectivity of~$h$. Moreover, $1<|h(\H_0)|<m$ is not possible either due to Lemma~\ref{lem:under-m}. Thus, $|h(\H_0)|=m$ and $h$ maps $\H_0$ to a copy of itself. As $(\H,\H_0)$ is endo-trivial, Lemma~\ref{lem:7} tells us that the restriction of $h$ to $\H$ is an automorphism of $\H$, which we call $\alpha$. The required retraction from $\G$ to $\H$ is now given by $\alpha^{-1} \circ h$.
nodes.statement_short: Exclude collapses of $\H_0$, then use pair endo-triviality to make $h|_\H$ an automorphism $\alpha$.

nodes.name: Generalised version of the copy-preservation lemma
nodes.statement: Let $\H_2 \supset \H_1 \supset H_0$ be a sequence of strongly connected reflexive tournaments, each one a subtournament of the one before. Suppose that any endomorphism of $\H_1$ that fixes $\H_0$ is an automorphism. Then any endomorphism $h$ of $\H_2$ that maps $\H_0$ to an isomorphic copy $\H'_0=i(\H_0)$ of itself also gives an isomorphic copy of $\H_1$ in $h(\H_1)$.
nodes.statement_short: In a tower $\H_0 \subset \H_1 \subset \H_2$, endomorphisms of $\H_2$ preserving a copy of $\H_0$ also preserve a copy of $\H_1$.
assumptions: Let $\H_2 \supset \H_1 \supset H_0$ be a sequence of strongly connected reflexive tournaments, each one a subtournament of the one before.
Suppose that any endomorphism of $\H_1$ that fixes $\H_0$ is an automorphism.
conclusions: any endomorphism $h$ of $\H_2$ that maps $\H_0$ to an isomorphic copy $\H'_0=i(\H_0)$ of itself also gives an isomorphic copy of $\H_1$ in $h(\H_1)$

nodes.name: Proof of the generalised copy-preservation lemma
nodes.statement: For contradiction, suppose there is an endomorphism $h$ of $\H_2$ that maps $\H_0$ to an isomorphic copy $\H'_0=i(\H_0)$ of itself that does not yield an isomorphic copy of $\H_1$. In particular, $|h(\H_1)|<|V(\H_1)|$. We proceed as in the proof of the Lemma~\ref{lem:7}. Choose $h^{-1}$ in the following fashion. We let $h^{-1}$ of $h(\H_0)$ be the natural isomorphism of $h(\H_0)$ to $\H_0$ (that inverts the isomorphism given by $h$ from $\H_0$ to $\H'_0$). Otherwise we choose $h^{-1}$ arbitrarily, such that $h^{-1}(y)=x$ only if $h(x)=y$. Since $\H_2$ is a reflexive tournament, $h^{-1}$ is an isomorphism. And $h^{-1} \circ h$ is an endomorphism of $\H_2$ that fixes $\H_0$ that does not yield an isomorphic copy of $\H_1$ in $h(\H_1)$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Same inverse-map construction as before, applied one level up in the tower.

nodes.name: Set up the contradiction
nodes.statement: For contradiction, suppose there is an endomorphism $h$ of $\H_2$ that maps $\H_0$ to an isomorphic copy $\H'_0=i(\H_0)$ of itself that does not yield an isomorphic copy of $\H_1$. In particular, $|h(\H_1)|<|V(\H_1)|$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $h$ shrinks $\H_1$.

nodes.name: Reuse the inverse-map construction
nodes.statement: We proceed as in the proof of the Lemma~\ref{lem:7}. Choose $h^{-1}$ in the following fashion. We let $h^{-1}$ of $h(\H_0)$ be the natural isomorphism of $h(\H_0)$ to $\H_0$ (that inverts the isomorphism given by $h$ from $\H_0$ to $\H'_0$). Otherwise we choose $h^{-1}$ arbitrarily, such that $h^{-1}(y)=x$ only if $h(x)=y$. Since $\H_2$ is a reflexive tournament, $h^{-1}$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Build $h^{-1}$ exactly as in the earlier lemma.

nodes.name: Derive the contradiction
nodes.statement: And $h^{-1} \circ h$ is an endomorphism of $\H_2$ that fixes $\H_0$ that does not yield an isomorphic copy of $\H_1$ in $h(\H_1)$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: $h^{-1}\circ h$ fixes $\H_0$ yet shrinks $\H_1$, contradicting the hypothesis.

nodes.name: General Case I
nodes.statement: Let $\H_{0},\H_{1}, \ldots, \H_k, \H_{k+1}$ be reflexive tournaments, the first $k$ of which have Hamilton cycles $\HC_{0},\HC_{1}, \ldots, \HC_{k}$, respectively, so that $\H_0 \subseteq H_1 \subseteq \cdots \subseteq \H_k \subseteq \H_{k+1}.$ Assume that $\H_0$, $(\H_1,\H_0)$, \ldots, $(\H_{k},\H_{k-1})$ are endo-trivial and that \[ \begin{array}{lcl} \mathrm{Spill}_{a_0}(\H_1[\H_0,\HC_{0}]) &= &V(\H_1) \\ \mathrm{Spill}_{a_1}(\H_2[\H_1,\HC_{1}]) &= &V(\H_2) \\ \hspace*{3mm} \vdots &\vdots &\hspace*{3mm}\vdots \\ \mathrm{Spill}_{a_{k-1}}(\H_{k}[\H_{k-1},\HC_{k-1}]) &= &V(\H_k).\\ \end{array} \] Assume that $\H_{k+1}$ retracts to $\H_k$ and also to every isomorphic copy $\H'_{k}=i(\H_k)$ of $\H_k$ in $\H_{k+1}$ with $\mathrm{Spill}_{a_k}(\H_{k+1}[\H'_k,i(\HC_{k})]) = V(\H_{k+1})$. Then $\H_k$-{\sc Retraction} can be polynomially reduced to {\sc Surjective $\H_{k+1}$-Colouring}.
nodes.statement_short: Tower version of Base Case I: a chain of endo-trivial pairs with full spills reduces $\H_k$-Retraction to Surjective $\H_{k+1}$-Colouring.
assumptions: Assume that $\H_0$, $(\H_1,\H_0)$, \ldots, $(\H_{k},\H_{k-1})$ are endo-trivial
Assume that $\H_{k+1}$ retracts to $\H_k$ and also to every isomorphic copy $\H'_{k}=i(\H_k)$ of $\H_k$ in $\H_{k+1}$ with $\mathrm{Spill}_{a_k}(\H_{k+1}[\H'_k,i(\HC_{k})]) = V(\H_{k+1})$.
conclusions: $\H_k$-{\sc Retraction} can be polynomially reduced to {\sc Surjective $\H_{k+1}$-Colouring}

nodes.name: Proof of General Case I
nodes.statement: Let $\G$ be an instance of {\sc $\H_k$-Retraction}. We will build an instance $\G''$ of {\sc Surjective $\H_{k+1}$-Colouring} in the following fashion. First, take a copy of $\H_{k+1}$ together with $\G$ and build $\G'$ by identifying these on the copy of $\H_{k}$ that they both possess as a subgraph. We now build $\G''$ as follows. First we augment $\G'$ with a new copy of $\Cyl_{a_k}$ for every vertex $v\in V(\G')\setminus V(\H_k)$. Vertex~$v$ is to be identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\DC^*_{a_k}$ in $\Cyl_{a_k}$, and the bottom copy of $\DC^*_{a_k}$ is to be identified with $\HC_k$ according to the identity function. Then, for each $i \in [k+1]$, and $v \in V(\H_{i}) \setminus V(\H_{i-1})$, add a copy of $\Cyl_{a_{i-1}}$, where $v$ is identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\DC^*_{a_{i-1}}$ in $\Cyl_{a_{i-1}}$ and the bottom copy of $\DC^*_{i-1}$ is to be identified with $\H_{i-1}$ according to the identity map of $\DC^*_{a_{i-1}}$ to $\HC_{i-1}$. We claim that $\G$ retracts to $\H_k$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\G''$ to $\H_{k+1}$. First suppose that $\G$ retracts to $\H_k$. Let $h$ be a retraction from $\G$ to $\H_{k}$. Extend $h$ mapping $\H_{k+1}$ according to the identity to ensure the final mapping is surjective. Finally, we map the various copies of $\Cyl_{a_{i-1}}$ in $\G''$ in any suitable fashion, which will always exist due to our assumptions and the fact that $\mathrm{Spill}_{a_{k}}(\H_{k+1}[\H_{k},\HC_{k}]) = V(\H_{k+1})$, which follows from our assumption that $\H_{k+1}$ retracts to $\H_k$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:spillage}. Now suppose that if there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\G''$ to $\H_{k+1}$. Suppose that $|h(\H_0)|=1$. Then $|h(\Cyl_{a_0})|=1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1}. Now we follow the chain of spills to deduce that $|h(\H_{k+1})|=1$, which is not possible. Now, $1<|h(\H_0)|<a_0$ is not possible either due to Lemma~\ref{lem:under-m}. Thus, $|h(\H_0)|=|V(\H_0)|$ and indeed $h$ maps $\H_0$ to a copy of itself in $\H_{k+1}$ which we will call $\H'_0=i(\H_0)$. We now apply Lemma~\ref{lem:8} as well as our assumed endo-trivialities to derive that $h$ in fact maps $\H_k$ by the isomorphism $i$ to a copy of itself in $\H_{k+1}$ which we will call $\H'_{k}$. nodes.name: Construct $\G''$ with gadgets at every level
nodes.statement: Let $\G$ be an instance of {\sc $\H_k$-Retraction}. We will build an instance $\G''$ of {\sc Surjective $\H_{k+1}$-Colouring} in the following fashion. First we augment $\G'$ with a new copy of $\Cyl_{a_k}$ for every vertex $v\in V(\G')\setminus V(\H_k)$. Vertex~$v$ is to be identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\DC^*_{a_k}$ in $\Cyl_{a_k}$, and the bottom copy of $\DC^*_{a_k}$ is to be identified with $\HC_k$ according to the identity function. Then, for each $i \in [k+1]$, and $v \in V(\H_{i}) \setminus V(\H_{i-1})$, add a copy of $\Cyl_{a_{i-1}}$, where $v$ is identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\DC^*_{a_{i-1}}$ in $\Cyl_{a_{i-1}}$ and the bottom copy of $\DC^*_{i-1}$ is to be identified with $\H_{i-1}$ according to the identity map of $\DC^*_{a_{i-1}}$ to $\HC_{i-1}$. nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: First suppose that $\G$ retracts to $\H_k$. Let $h$ be a retraction from $\G$ to $\H_{k}$. nodes.name: Backward direction via the chain of spills
nodes.statement: Now suppose that if there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\G''$ to $\H_{k+1}$. Suppose that $|h(\H_0)|=1$. Then $|h(\Cyl_{a_0})|=1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1}. Now we follow the chain of spills to deduce that $|h(\H_{k+1})|=1$, which is not possible. Now, $1<|h(\H_0)|<a_0$ is not possible either due to Lemma~\ref{lem:under-m}. Thus, $|h(\H_0)|=|V(\H_0)|$ and indeed $h$ maps $\H_0$ to a copy of itself in $\H_{k+1}$ which we will call $\H'_0=i(\H_0)$. Now $i^{-1} \circ r \circ h$ gives the desired retraction of $\G''$ to $\H_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Collapse of $\H_0$ propagates up the tower and is impossible; then Lemma 8 lifts the copy of $\H_0$ to $\H_k$.

nodes.name: General Case II
nodes.statement: Let $\H_{0},\H_{1}, \ldots, \H_k, \H_{k+1}$ be reflexive tournaments, the first $k+1$ of which have Hamilton cycles $\HC_{0},\HC_{1}, \ldots, \HC_{k}$, respectively, so that $\H_0 \subseteq H_1 \subseteq \cdots \subseteq \H_k \subseteq \H_{k+1}$. Suppose that $\H_0$, $(\H_1,\H_0)$, \ldots, $(\H_{k},\H_{k-1}), (\H_{k+1},\H_{k})$ are endo-trivial and that \[ \begin{array}{lcl} \mathrm{Spill}_{a_0}(\H_1[\H_0,\HC_{0}]) &= &V(\H_1) \\ \mathrm{Spill}_{a_1}(\H_2[\H_1,\HC_{1}]) &= &V(\H_2) \\ \hspace*{3mm} \vdots &\vdots &\hspace*{3mm}\vdots \\ \mathrm{Spill}_{a_{k-1}}(\H_{k}[\H_{k-1},\HC_{k-1}]) &= &V(\H_k)\\ \mathrm{Spill}_{a_{k}}(\H_{k+1}[\H_{k},\HC_{k}]) &= &V(\H_{k+1}) \end{array} \] Then {\sc $\H_{k+1}$-Retraction} can be polynomially reduced to {\sc Surjective $\H_{k+1}$-Colouring}.

assumptions: Suppose that $\H_0$, $(\H_1,\H_0)$, \ldots, $(\H_{k},\H_{k-1}), (\H_{k+1},\H_{k})$ are endo-trivial
conclusions: {\sc $\H_{k+1}$-Retraction} can be polynomially reduced to {\sc Surjective $\H_{k+1}$-Colouring}

nodes.name: Proof of General Case II
nodes.statement: Let $\G$ be an instance of {\sc $\H_{k+1}$-Retraction}. We build an instance $\G'$ of {\sc Surjective $\H_{k+1}$-Colouring} in the following fashion. Build $\G'$ by, for each $i \in [k+1]$, and $v \in V(\H_{i}) \setminus V(\H_{i-1})$, adding a copy of $\Cyl_{a_{i-1}}$, where $v$ is identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\DC^*_{a_{i-1}}$ in $\Cyl_{a_{i-1}}$ and the bottom copy of $\DC^*_{i-1}$ is to be identified with $\H_{i-1}$ according to the identity map of $\DC^*_{a_{i-1}}$ to $\HC_{i-1}$. We claim that $\G$ retracts to $\H_{k+1}$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\G'$ to $\H_{k+1}$. First suppose that $\G$ retracts to $\H_{k+1}$. Let $h$ be a retraction from $\G$ to $\H_{k+1}$. Then we can extend $h$ by mapping $\G'$ in some suitable fashion, which is possible due to the spill assumptions. Now suppose that there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\G'$ to $\H_{k+1}$. Suppose that $|h(\H_0)|=1$. Then $|h(\Cyl_{a_0})|=1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1}. nodes.name: Forward direction

nodes.name: Backward direction
nodes.statement: Now suppose that there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\G'$ to $\H_{k+1}$. Suppose that $|h(\H_0)|=1$. Then $|h(\Cyl_{a_0})|=1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1}. Now we follow the chain of spills to deduce that $|h(\H_{k+1})|=1$, a contradiction. Now, $1<|h(\H_0)|<a_0$ is not possible either due to Lemma~\ref{lem:under-m}. The required retraction from $\G'$ to $\H_{k+1}$ is now given by $\alpha^{-1} \circ h$.
nodes.statement_short: Rule out collapses, lift the $\H_0$-copy to $\H_k$ via Lemma 8, then get an automorphism $\alpha$ via Lemma 7.

nodes.name: Hardness for strongly connected reflexive tournaments
nodes.statement: Let $\H$ be a strongly connected reflexive tournament. Then {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring} is \NP-complete.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
assumptions: Let $\H$ be a strongly connected reflexive tournament.
conclusions: Then {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring} is \NP-complete.

nodes.name: Proof of hardness for strongly connected reflexive tournaments
nodes.statement: As $\H$ is is a strongly connected reflexive tournament, which has more than one vertex by our definition, $\H$ is not transitive. Note that {\sc $\H$-Retraction} is \NP-complete, since non-transitive reflexive tournaments omit Taylor polymorphisms~\cite{larose2006taylor}, following Theorem~\ref{thm:ret-hardness}. Thus, if $\H$ is endo-trivial, the result follows from Lemma~\ref{prop:main1} (note that we could also have used Corollary~\ref{c-main}). Suppose $\H$ is not endo-trivial. Then, by Lemma~\ref{lem:endo-retraction-trivial}, $\H$ is not retract-trivial either. This means $\H$ has a non-trivial retraction to some subtournament~$\H_0$. We may assume that $\H_0$ is endo-trivial, as otherwise we will repeat the argument until we find a retraction from $\H$ to an endo-trivial subtournament. If $\H$ retracts to all isomorphic copies $\H'_0=i(\H_0)$ of $\H_0$ within it, except possibly those for which $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H'_0,i(\HC_0)]) \neq V(\H)$, then the result follows from Lemma~\ref{prop:main1}. So there is a copy $\H'_0=i(\H'_0)$ to which $\H$ does not retract for which $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H'_0,i(\HC_0)]) = V(\H)$. If $(\H,\H'_0)$ is endo-trivial, the result follows from Lemma~\ref{prop:main2}. Thus we assume $(\H,\H'_0)$ is not endo-trivial and we deduce the existence of $\H'_0 \subset \H_1 \subset \H$ ($\H_1$ is strictly between $\H$ and $\H'_0$) so that $(\H_1,\H'_0)$ is endotrivial and $\H$ retracts to $\H_1$. Now we are ready to break out. Either $\H$ retracts to all isomorphic copies of $\H'_1=i(\H_1)$ in $\H$, except possibly for those so that $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H'_1,i(\HC_1)]) \neq V(\H)$, and we apply Lemma~\ref{prop:main-general1}, or there exists a copy $\H'_1$, with $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\H[\H'_1,i(\HC_1)]) = V(\H)$, to which it does not retract. Then $\H'_1$ contains $\H''_0$ a copy of $\H''_0$ so that $(\H'_1,\H''_0)$ and $\H''_0$ are endo-trivial. We now continue iterating this method, which will terminate because our structures are getting strictly larger.

nodes.statement_short: Iterate: either an endo-trivial retract lets Base/General Case I apply, or a non-retracting full-spill copy pushes the argument one level up the strictly growing tower.

nodes.statement: Let $\H$ be a strongly connected reflexive tournament. Then {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring} is \NP-complete even for strongly connected digraphs.

nodes.name: Proof that the constructed instances may be assumed strongly connected
nodes.statement: We need to argue that the instances of {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring} that we have constructed before can be assumed to be strongly connected. Noting that $\H$ and the gadgets $\Cylm$ are strongly connected, this is clear once we can assume the inputs to our Retraction problems are strongly connected. For {\sc $\H'$-Retraction}, where $\H'$ is a strongly connected reflexive tournament, we can surely assume our inputs are strongly connected. If they were not, then we add individual directed paths of length $|V(\H')|$ between the relevant vertices. This will not affect the truth of an instance and the result follows.

nodes.statement_short: Pad retraction inputs with directed paths of length $|V(\H')|$ to make them strongly connected without changing the answer.

nodes.name: standard decomposition of a reflexive tournament into strong components
nodes.statement: When $\G$ is a reflexive tournament, we may break it up into strongly connected components $\G(1),\ldots,\G(k)$ so that, for all $i < j \in [k]$, for all $x \in \G(i)$ and for all $y \in \G(j)$, $(x,y) \in E(\G)$. This is the standard decomposition, inducing a standard order on the connected components, that we will use.

nodes.name: Hardness for all non-transitive reflexive tournaments
nodes.statement: Let $\H$ be a non-transitive reflexive tournament. Then {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring} is \NP-complete.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
assumptions: Let $\H$ be a non-transitive reflexive tournament.
conclusions: {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring} is \NP-complete

nodes.name: Proof of hardness for non-transitive reflexive tournaments
nodes.statement: For strongly connected tournaments, the result follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:strongly-connected1}. Let $\H$ instead have $k>1$ strongly connected components $\H(1),\ldots,\H(k)$. Since $\H$ is not transitive, one of these strongly connected components, $\H(i)$, must be of size greater than $1$, whereupon we know from Corollary~\ref{cor:strongly-connected2} that {\sc Surjective $\H(i)$-Colouring} is \NP-complete, even when restricted to strongly connected inputs. Let us reduce {\sc Surjective $\H(i)$-Colouring} to {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring} by taking a strongly connected input $\G$ for the former and building $\G'$ by adding a copy of $\H$ restricted to $V(\H(1)),\ldots,V(\H(i-1))$, where every vertex here has an edge to every vertex of $\G$, and adding a copy of $\H$ restricted to $V(\H(i+1)),\ldots,V(\H(k))$, where every vertex there has an edge from every vertex of $\G$. Note that $\G'$ has $k$ strongly connected components $\G'(1),\ldots, \G'(k)$, where $\G'(h)$ is isomorphic to $\H'(h)$ for $h=1,\ldots,k$, $h\neq i$. We claim that there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\G$ to $\H(i)$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\G'$ to $\H$. (Forwards.) Map the additional vertices in $\G'$ in the obvious fashion (by the ``identity'') to extend a surjective homomorphism from $\G$ to $\H_i$ so that it is surjective from $\G'$ to $\H$. (Backwards.) In any surjective homomorphism $s$ from $\G'$ to $\H$, we have that $s(V(\G'(i))) \subseteq V(\H(i))$ for $i=1,\ldots k$.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Reduce from the hard strongly connected component $\H(i)$ by sandwiching an input between copies of the remaining components.

nodes.name: Locate a non-trivial strong component
nodes.statement: For strongly connected tournaments, the result follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:strongly-connected1}. Let $\H$ instead have $k>1$ strongly connected components $\H(1),\ldots,\H(k)$. Since $\H$ is not transitive, one of these strongly connected components, $\H(i)$, must be of size greater than $1$, whereupon we know from Corollary~\ref{cor:strongly-connected2} that {\sc Surjective $\H(i)$-Colouring} is \NP-complete, even when restricted to strongly connected inputs.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Non-transitivity gives a strong component $\H(i)$ of size $>1$, hard even on strongly connected inputs.

nodes.name: Build the reduction instance $\G'$
nodes.statement: Let us reduce {\sc Surjective $\H(i)$-Colouring} to {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring} by taking a strongly connected input $\G$ for the former and building $\G'$ by adding a copy of $\H$ restricted to $V(\H(1)),\ldots,V(\H(i-1))$, where every vertex here has an edge to every vertex of $\G$, and adding a copy of $\H$ restricted to $V(\H(i+1)),\ldots,V(\H(k))$, where every vertex there has an edge from every vertex of $\G$. Note that $\G'$ has $k$ strongly connected components $\G'(1),\ldots, \G'(k)$, where $\G'(h)$ is isomorphic to $\H'(h)$ for $h=1,\ldots,k$, $h\neq i$. We claim that there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\G$ to $\H(i)$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\G'$ to $\H$.

nodes.statement_short: Sandwich $\G$ between copies of the earlier and later components of $\H$, all edges crossing.

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: (Forwards.) Map the additional vertices in $\G'$ in the obvious fashion (by the ``identity'') to extend a surjective homomorphism from $\G$ to $\H_i$ so that it is surjective from $\G'$ to $\H$.

nodes.statement_short: Extend by the identity on the added components.

nodes.name: Backward direction
nodes.statement: (Backwards.) In any surjective homomorphism $s$ from $\G'$ to $\H$, we have that $s(V(\G'(i))) \subseteq V(\H(i))$ for $i=1,\ldots k$.

nodes.name: Dichotomy for {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring} on reflexive tournaments
nodes.statement: Let $\H$ be a reflexive tournament. If $\H$ is transitive, then {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring} is in \NL; otherwise it is \NP-complete.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Main result: transitive reflexive tournaments give \NL, all others \NP-complete.

If $\H$ is transitive

nodes.name: Proof of the reflexive-tournament dichotomy
nodes.statement: For the transitive case we can say that {\sc \H-Retraction} is in \NL\ from \cite{DalmauK08}, since $\H$ enjoys the ternary median operation as a polymorphism (this has been observed, inter alia, in \cite{larose2006taylor}). It follows of course that {\sc Surjective $\H$-Colouring} is in \NL\ also. The non-transitive case follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:hauptsatz}.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
